extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under Step 2B (Alice/Mayo framework), including what counts as well‑understood, routine, conventional activity and what constitutes meaningful limitations or mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity. This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, and insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider whether elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry, and analyze elements both individually and in combination. Use other Step 2B considerations (MPEP § 2106.05(a),(f),(g)) to assist the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-in-art can still be unconventional/non-routine
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/obviousness inquiries are 'fully apart' from eligibility; claims may improve conventional functionality even if anticipated by prior art (e.g., Enfish). Examine whether claimed features provide benefits/technical improvements (flexibility, speed, reduced memory, etc.) that render them non-conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual determination required and must be supported in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual determination is required to support a conclusion that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate support forms include: (a) citation to specification or applicant statements; (b) citation to court decisions recognizing the element as conventional; (c) citation to publications demonstrating conventionality; or (d) examiner taking official notice. The required factual determination must be expressly supported in writing (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)). Prior art searches are not always necessary; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize as conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of additional elements may amount to an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one or more additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity when considered individually, the combination of additional elements may amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new combination of known steps may be patentable (Diamond v. Diehr). Evaluate combinations for unconventional, non-generic arrangements that provide technical improvements (e.g., BASCOM, Rapid Litigation Management). Consider whether combined elements perform functions that are not merely generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection only when examiner can conclude 'no' on significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should only be made if an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art can conclude in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements or functions are beyond those recognized in the art or by the courts as conventional, they will in most cases amount to significantly more (Step 2B: YES). Examiners may explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer functions courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner (e.g., at a high level of generality) or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: receiving or transmitting data over a network (using Internet to gather data), performing repetitive calculations, electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts), storing and retrieving information in memory, electronically scanning/extracting data (OCR), and web browser back/forward button functionality. However, not all computer functions are conventional; generic recitation of computer components may be insufficient, whereas non-generic combinations or technical improvements can be significantly more (see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory techniques courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed in a merely generic manner or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means, using PCR to amplify/detect DNA, detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample, immunizing a patient, analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants, freezing and thawing cells, amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids, and hybridizing a gene probe. Generic recitation of these techniques may not render a claim significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found other ordinary activities to be well-understood, routine, or conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include recording a customer's order, shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards, restricting access by requiring viewing an advertisement, presenting offers and gathering statistics, determining an estimated outcome and setting a price, and arranging/sorting information to determine prices. Analyze these activities in context and relative to other Step 2B considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations must add meaningful limitations beyond mere linking
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations are those that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception or integrate the exception into a practical application. Considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) may qualify as meaningful limitations. Examples: Diehr (Arrhenius equation integrated into rubber-molding process) and Classen (analysis step plus immunization step integrated into specific application). Mere implementation via computers or routine data-gathering generally does not meaningfully limit an abstract idea (see Alice, OIP Technologies). Evaluate elements individually and in combination; treatment/prophylaxis limitations overlap with Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Another consideration is whether additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible (Alice; Mayo; Benson). Requiring more than mere instructions does not mean claims must be narrow—some broad claims are eligible if they recite non-generic, technical improvements (e.g., McRO, Thales Visionix). Beware analyses that turn on 'the draftsman’s art.'
